questions.q: What is the fundamental structural difference between a columnstore index and every rowstore index (clustered, nonclustered, covering, filtered) from earlier in this chapter?
options: Columnstore stores each column together, compressed independently across all rows, instead of storing each row's columns together
Columnstore indexes cannot be created on any table larger than 1 million rows
Columnstore indexes don't support compression at all
There is no structural difference; columnstore is just a naming convention
questions.explain: Rowstore indexes are row-major (a row's columns stored together); columnstore indexes are column-major (a column's values stored together across all rows).

questions.q: Why does columnstore suit a query like `SELECT ProductCategory, SUM(SalesAmount) FROM FactSales GROUP BY ProductCategory` on a huge fact table?
options: The query only touches a few columns across millions of rows, and columnstore reads and compresses just those columns rather than every column of every row
GROUP BY queries are not supported on rowstore indexes at all
Columnstore indexes automatically pre-aggregate SUM results at index build time
SalesAmount must always be the clustering key for aggregates to work
questions.explain: Columnstore's column-major layout means an aggregate touching few columns over many rows reads only those columns, and benefits from same-typed compression.

questions.q: What are the two mechanisms this lesson credits for columnstore's analytical speed?
options: Compression (same-typed column values stored together) and batch mode execution (processing rows in batches of roughly 900 at a time)
Row-level locking and synchronous replication
Automatic index defragmentation and TRUNCATE-only writes
In-memory OLTP and natively compiled stored procedures
questions.explain: The lesson specifically names compression from column-major storage and batch mode execution as the two mechanisms behind columnstore's analytical performance.

questions.q: Why is a columnstore index the wrong tool for an OLTP table hit by thousands of single-row lookups per second?
options: Reconstructing a single row means pulling from multiple separately compressed column segments and stitching them back together, which is more expensive than a rowstore seek
Columnstore indexes cannot store primary key columns
SQL Server limits columnstore indexes to read-only tables
Columnstore indexes always require a full table scan for every query, with no exceptions
questions.explain: Columnstore's advantages come from scanning many rows across few columns; reassembling one full row from compressed column segments is comparatively expensive.

questions.q: What is the difference between a clustered columnstore index and a nonclustered columnstore index?
options: A clustered columnstore index becomes the table's primary storage; a nonclustered columnstore index is an additional analytical copy alongside an existing rowstore table
A nonclustered columnstore index can only be created on views, never on tables
A clustered columnstore index is always slower than a nonclustered one
They are identical in every respect except their name
questions.explain: Clustered columnstore replaces the table's storage entirely; nonclustered columnstore sits beside a rowstore table so OLTP writes and analytical reads can be served differently.
